title: Quality of service (QoS): classification, queues and priorities

videos.script: An office has one internet line, and somebody starts uploading a large file. {{upload}} A moment later the call in the next room starts to break up. The line is not broken. It is full, and the call is waiting behind the file. {{queue}} In this lesson you make that happen on purpose. The lab's uplink becomes a five megabit link, with a queue of a hundred packets in front of it. {{ping}} An idle ping takes a fraction of a millisecond. During an upload, the slowest reply takes two hundred and twenty. {{mark}} Then you try the obvious fix. You mark the ping as voice. It changes nothing, because nothing reads the mark yet. {{classes}} So you build what reads it. A classifier, a queue for each class, and a scheduler that sends voice first. The marked ping drops back to the idle figure, while the upload carries on beside it. {{trust}} Then the uncomfortable part. Anyone can mark their own packets as voice. So the router at the edge wipes every mark, and writes back only the ones it trusts. {{internet}} And you will see where all of this stops. At the edge of the links you own.
